relations.note: He pursues the Anjanas, but they evade capture by becoming invisible.

relations.myth: The daily works of the Anjanas
relations.note: Anjanas repair natural damage caused by Ojáncanos and embody their moral opposite.
Later systematizations contrast the beneficent Anjana with the destructive female ogress.
Modern regional mythographies present the Cantabrian Anjana as the Xana's counterpart.
Llano argued writers imported and reshaped Basajaun as the Busgosu.
Basajaun substitutes for or represents Gaueko as the nocturnal abductor.
relations.source: Lower Navarre/Beyrie oral versions summarized by Barandiarán

relations.note: A literary fiction depicts angry xanas transforming themselves into cuélebres.
The cuélebre guards treasure and imprisons an enchanted Xana in later syntheses.

relations.myth: Guardians of the xanas’ subterranean riches
relations.note: Cuélebres guard the xanas’ palaces and riches from mortal access.
Later systematic accounts represent the female Moon as Eguzki's sister.
Some modern accounts make Mari Eguzki's mother, often by identifying Mari with Earth or Amalur.
Jentilak abduct Kattalin and proclaim Gaueko’s night-rule as his interpreted instruments.
Folklorists proposed equation or motif-transfer between the two serpentine beings.

relations.myth: The Grateful Tartaro and the Heren-Suge
relations.note: Tartalo equips and advises Petit Yorge to defeat Heren-Suge.

relations.myth: The Grateful Tartaro and the Heren-Suge
relations.note: Tartaro helps equip the hero who later kills Herensuge; they never interact directly.
relations.source: Webster, The Grateful Tartaro and the Heren-Suge

relations.note: Barandiarán identified the survivor who announces Christ’s birth with Olentzero.
Later systematization identifies Olentzero as the lone jentil survivor who announces Kixmi.
Some Souletin traditions describe maide as the husbands of lamias.
Modern pageantry places Mari and the lamiak together in a festive drama.
Modern mythological pageantry presents Sugaar and the lamiak as separate characters.
Caro Baroja compares Basque lamia stories with corresponding Asturian Xana traditions.

relations.myth: Mari and Maju meet on Fridays
relations.note: Mari’s husband visits her; their union produces violent rain and hail.
The serpent-like Sugaar is Mari’s husband; their meeting causes storms.
Maju is explicitly described as Mari's husband in Azkoitia tradition.
Maju visits Mari on Friday afternoons and combs her hair.
Maju visits Mari on Friday afternoons to comb her hair.
Maju meets Mari on Fridays, and their union produces a violent storm.

relations.myth: Meigas and Santa Compaña share supernatural imagery
relations.note: They appear together in modern imagery and the queimada text without a stable narrative relation.
Galician lexicography treats the moura encantada as the Xana's regional equivalent.

Aherbelste.note: Modern scholarship proposes Aherbelste as Akerbeltz’s linguistic predecessor, but historical identity remains unproved.

Akerbeltz.note: Modern retellings sometimes portray Akerbeltz as Mari’s servant.
Modern retellings sometimes portray Akerbeltz as Mari’s consort.

Ama Lur.note: Later mythographic synthesis presents Earth as Ilargi’s mother.

Ama Lur.myth: Earth creates Moon to protect humans from nocturnal beings
Ama Lur.note: Expanded modern cosmogony says Earth deliberately created Ilargi as protection.

Ama Lur.myth: Moon returns nightly into Earth after crossing the sky
Ama Lur.note: Later synthesis extends the celestial earth-return motif to Ilargi.

Amalur.note: Modern accounts present Eguzki and Ilargi as daughters of Amalur.
In the modern synthetic legend, Amalur creates Eguzki to repel nocturnal beings.
Modern philosophical and popular literature identifies Mari with Mother Earth, Amalur.

Andobellicus.note: Name similarity prompted a disputed theory of identity or related local hypostases.

Atarrabi.note: Some versions make the beneficent guardian Atarrabi Mari’s child.
Modern mythographies call Atarrabi Sugaar's son, but early localized testimony is unverified.

Atto.note: Atto journeys with Sugaar through Euskal Herria in a children's story.

Axular.note: Axular sometimes replaces or accompanies Atarrabi among the cave-school companions.

Ayalgas.note: Cuélebres block access to the ayalgas’ fabulous wealth and palaces.

Basandere.note: Basandere is repeatedly described as Basajaun's wife and supernatural accomplice.

Berstuk.note: Menéndez Pidal included Berstuk among Slavic beings equated with Asturian Busgosos.

Candamo.note: Popular synthesis alleges that the Asturian horned god evolved into Busgosu.

Christian God.note: Modern summaries describe the Moon as God’s face.

Cosus.note: Modern scholarship proposes both as regional names for similar protective or martial power.

Culebro.note: Later interpretation identifies Sugaar with the medieval Biscayan serpent-demon Culebro.

Diañu Burlón.note: This mischievous devil overlaps with the Trasgu, especially outdoors, but early collectors distinguish them.

Duende.note: Early-modern lexicography treats duende as an ordinary Spanish equivalent and umbrella category.

Earth.note: Barandiarán interpreted Earth as the mother to whom Eguzki returns nightly.

Eate.note: Eate moves destructive weather as a subordinate associated with Mari.

Eguzki.note: Modern handbooks commonly present Moon and Sun as Earth’s sister daughters.

Eluauso.note: Eluauso is named among Mari’s storm-directing subordinate beings.

Etxajaun.note: Landucci presents the Basque household being as a translation-equivalent of drasgo or duende.

Guirrio.note: Cabal linked masked Guirrio traditions with the Busgosu and Faun pattern.

Gurmantes.note: Gurmantes capture a cuélebre while a hailstorm is expected.

Haxerihargaitz.myth: The theft of marvellous golden objects
Haxerihargaitz.note: The trickster Haxerihargaitz steals wondrous golden possessions from Basajauns.

Hodei.note: Internet-era summaries claim the rival Hodei killed Mari; ethnographic support is absent.

Horned God.note: Modern witchcraft and occult reception treat Akerbeltz as an analogue of the Horned God.

Jaun Zuria.note: Modern retellings make Sugaar the founder's father by identifying him with Culebro.

Jayanes.myth: Joint guardians of the xanas’ riches
Jayanes.note: Cuélebres and jayanes jointly guard the subterranean riches of the xanas.

Jentil.note: A jentil occupies Tartalo's role in a speaking-ring escape variant.

Jesus.myth: The charcoal burner announces Jesus’s birth
Jesus.note: Olentzero returns from the mountain and proclaims that Jesus has been born.
Later retellings make Olentzero the surviving jentil who spreads news of Christ’s arrival.

Jesus Christ.note: As the sabbath Devil, Aker allegedly instructs initiates not to utter Jesus’s name.

Jesus Christ.myth: Kixmi’s birth ends the Jentil age
Jesus Christ.note: Their blind elder recognizes a portent of Christ’s birth and foretells their destruction.

Jesus Christ.myth: Christ's baptism is invoked in a healing formula
Jesus Christ.note: Ana de Castro invoked Christ's baptism in the Jordan while performing a cure.

Kobold.note: Folklorists compare the Trasgu with Germanic kobolds while proposing speculative origin theories.

Lutin.note: Oudin translates trasgo through French household-spirit terms lutin and esprit follet.

Mari Domingi.note: Mari Domingi works alongside Olentzero as an autonomous co-gift-bringer.
Later portrayals sometimes call her his wife or girlfriend, controversially and without traditional basis.

Marije Kobako.note: Markina tradition calls Marije Kobako the sister of the Lady of Anboto.
Marije Kobako and the Lady of Anboto travel to visit one another.

Mikelats.note: Some accounts make the destructive storm-maker Mikelats Mari’s child.
Mikelats replaces Sugoi in an analogous Sara version; they never meet.
Modern mythographies call Mikelats Sugaar's son, but early localized testimony is unverified.

Musgosu.note: Later regional syntheses increasingly conflate the Cantabrian woodland helper with Busgosu.

Nuberos.note: Men called nuberos enter potholes and draw blood from cuélebres.

Odei.note: Odei directs clouds or weather on Mari’s behalf in Barandiarán’s synthesis.

Polkan.note: Menéndez Pidal equated Polkans with the Busgosos of Asturias.

Providence.note: Providence initiates the divine arrangements within the drama containing the Moura Encantada.

Ramidreju.note: Anjanas drink its gall, which cures disease and reveals buried treasure.

Robin Goodfellow.note: An early-modern bilingual dictionary uses Robin Goodfellow and hobgoblin as English equivalents.

Saint Anthony.note: Hartsuaga proposes Saint Anthony as a Christianized successor to the livestock-protecting Basajaun.

Saint Clare.myth: Lunar greeting becomes a Christianized Saint Clare song
Saint Clare.note: At Ondarroa, Saint Clare substitutes for Moon in the greeting formula.
Saint Clare.source: Barandiarán, La religion des anciens Basques

Saint John.myth: John appears in a formula against magical affliction
Saint John.note: Saint John appears in Ana de Castro's cure and later protective seasonal folklore.

Saint Marina.note: Folklorists propose Saint Marina as a Christianized survival or analogue of Mari.

Saint Peter.myth: Peter accompanies Christ in a healing formula
Saint Peter.note: Ana de Castro's formula describes Saint Peter holding Christ by the hand.

San Martín Txiki.myth: Leap across the Basajauns' wheat heap
San Martín Txiki.note: San Martín challenges the Basajauns to leap across their grain heap.

San Martín Txiki.myth: The theft of wheat at Muskia
San Martín Txiki.note: San Martín steals the Basajauns' wheat by filling his broad sandals.
San Martín secretly overhears a Basajaun's song explaining when crops should be sown.
San Martín's false claim induces Basajaun to reveal the chestnut-leaf model.
Trying to spoil the saw, Basajaun accidentally improves it by alternating its teeth.
San Martín tricks or overhears Basajaun into revealing a welding or foundry technique.
San Martín falsely claims success, prompting Basajaun to reveal the missing mill component.

Satyrs.note: His goatlike body and pursuit of women prompted comparison with satyrs.
Satyrs.source: Jove, Mitos y supersticiones de Asturias

Sorginak.note: Eguzki's light or floral representation blocks, immobilizes, or repels supernatural witches.
Witches seize María and recite the formula assigning night to night-beings.

Suarra.note: This Betelu serpent figure was compared with Sugaar, Mari’s partner.

Sugoi.note: Collectors equated this Dima serpent being with Sugaar, Mari’s partner.

Sumiciu.note: Cabal treats Sumiciu as a specialized Trasgu, while de Llano questions its independent personification.

The Virgin Mary.myth: Mary is invoked in cures against meigallo
The Virgin Mary.note: Healing formulas invoke Mary, while O Corpiño pilgrims seek her intercession against meigallo.

Trasno.note: Trasno is the Galician and western Asturian regional form of the household-spirit complex.

Urtzi.note: Modern mythographic systems sometimes place Mari in conflict with this sky god.

Vaelicus.note: Proposed as a linguistically related or identical regional deity; the identity remains disputed.

Vellicus.note: Name similarity prompted a disputed theory of identity or related local hypostases.

Virgin Mary.note: As the sabbath Devil, Aker allegedly requires initiates to renounce or avoid invoking the Virgin.
Local Christian explanations identify the Virgin as Eguzki's mother and nightly destination.
Mari is interpreted as the Virgin’s pre-Christian counterpart or Christianized substitute.

Vosegus.note: Modern speculation proposes Vosegus as a name or functional ancestor.

enchanted maiden.myth: The Anjana beneath the river pool
enchanted maiden.note: The Anjana gives a woodcutter instructions for releasing the maiden from a tree.

incubus.note: Nebrija translates the domestic drasgo with the classical demonological term incubus.

lamina of Mondarrain.note: Eguzki's first ray halts the lamina's pursuit and forces her into her cave.

lemures.note: Learned writers compare the Trasgu with classical lemures; no narrative encounter is recorded.

nymph.note: Writers classify the Xana by analogy with classical water nymphs and ondines.

olano.note: Three intelligent dog-like olano serve as extraordinary messenger-beasts.

xanín.note: Xanas bear xaninos, sometimes exchanging them for human infants.
